hints: Focus on what two different silver halide precipitates could form here, and how each one behaves in ammonia.
Check the moles: you have 0.00025 mol of Cl- and 0.00025 mol of I- reacting with 0.00050 mol of Ag+, so both AgCl and AgI form at first.
Remember the solubility rule in concentrated ammonia: AgCl dissolves, AgBr only dissolves in concentrated, but AgI stays solid, so think about which colour is left behind.
walkthrough:
**Find the moles of each halide and silver ion**

Think of this as checking if there is enough silver to catch both halides. Moles = concentration x volume in dm3.

$$n(\text{Cl}^-) = 0.05 \times \frac{5}{1000} = 2.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$
$$n(\text{I}^-) = 0.05 \times \frac{5}{1000} = 2.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$
$$n(\text{Ag}^+) = 0.05 \times \frac{10}{1000} = 5.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$

**Write what precipitates first**

Silver ions love halides, and there is exactly enough for both. You get a mixture of two solids.

$$\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(s) \text{ white}$$
$$\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{I}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgI}(s) \text{ yellow}$$

**Apply the ammonia test**

This is the classic distinguishing test. AgCl dissolves easily even in dilute $\text{NH}_3$ to form the complex $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+$. AgI is insoluble even in excess concentrated $\text{NH}_3$.

$$\text{AgCl}(s) + 2\text{NH}_3(aq) \rightarrow [\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq) \text{ dissolves}$$
$$\text{AgI}(s) + \text{NH}_3(aq) \rightarrow \text{no reaction, stays as solid}$$

**Conclude what is seen**

The white AgCl disappears into a colourless solution, leaving only the yellow AgI behind. So after excess concentrated ammonia, a yellow precipitate remains.

options.A: Cream is the colour of $\text{AgBr}$. No bromide ions were added here, only chloride from NaCl and iodide from KI, so this is a classic colour confusion trap.
options.B: White is the colour of $\text{AgCl}$, which does form at first. However $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves in dilute and concentrated ammonia to give $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+$, so it will not be seen at the end.
options.C: Yellow is the colour of $\text{AgI}$. Both precipitates form initially, but only $\text{AgI}$ is insoluble in excess concentrated ammonia, so it is the solid left visible.
options.D: It is tempting to think concentrated ammonia dissolves everything. It dissolves $\text{AgCl}$ completely, but $\text{AgI}$ is too insoluble to dissolve, so a precipitate remains.
